title: Reactive Devaluation
text:
In the 1980s students at Stanford University campaigned for the university to sell its investments in companies doing business in apartheid-era South Africa. The university eventually announced a policy of partial divestment. Lee Ross and Constance Stillinger used the debate to study a barrier to resolving conflicts.

The researchers asked students to evaluate two possible plans: the partial divestment that the university had adopted, and an alternative plan that set a deadline for total divestment if conditions in South Africa did not improve. Some students were surveyed before the university announced its choice; others afterwards. Before the announcement, students rated the plans roughly according to their content. Once the university adopted partial divestment, students rated it less favorably than before, while the alternative plan, the one not offered, rose in their eyes. A proposal became less attractive simply because the other side had put it on the table.

In related studies by Ross and colleagues, Americans rated a nuclear arms reduction proposal less favorably when they were told it came from the Soviet leader than when told it came from the American president.

Ross and Stillinger called this reactive devaluation. In conflicts, people assume that anything their opponent offers must benefit the opponent, and therefore must be less valuable to them. Concessions lose value at the very moment they are offered, which can block agreements both sides would otherwise accept.
lesson: When an opponent offers a concession, judge it on its merits as if it came from a neutral party. Distrust of the source can make you reject a deal you would otherwise welcome.
source: Ross, L., and Stillinger, C. (1991). Barriers to conflict resolution. Negotiation Journal, 7(4), 389-404.
